title: Can they pay for one?
principle: People look at the price of one use. A small pack lets more people buy, even if each gram costs a little more.

screens.text: Let me tell you about Chinni Krishnan. He lived in Cuddalore, in Tamil Nadu. In the 1970s, good shampoo was costly. Workers paid by the week bought only what lasted a day or a week. He said, "Whatever I make, I want the coolies and the rickshaw pullers to use."

screens.title: One wash at a time
screens.text: So he packed shampoo in tiny packets, called sachets. Each held enough for one use. A worker couldn't pay for a big pack, but he could buy one sachet. Later, his youngest son, C.K. Ranganathan, started his own shampoo, Chik, and sold it in sachets too.

screens.prompt: In 1999, Chik had 6 of every 100 shampoo sales, and sold a 50-paise sachet. By 2003, how many of every 100 were Chik's?
screens.why: About 23, about four times as many. Local radio ads and a strong scent helped too. But the 50-paise sachet let many people buy shampoo for the first time.

screens.title: A bit more for each piece
screens.text: Village shopkeepers did the same with soap. In the 1970s, one shopkeeper cut a bar of Lifebuoy soap into six pieces. The six pieces together cost a little more than the whole bar. People still bought them, because they could pay for one piece today.

screens.title: The sachet idea
screens.text: A famous business professor, C.K. Prahalad, wrote about small packs for poorer buyers. Many buyers ask, "Can I pay for one use today?", not "How much is it per kilo?" A small pack lets them say yes, even if each gram costs a little more.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Shampoo is a giant market, but the same idea works in your home bakery, where you bake cakes for families nearby. It's April of your third year. Students in a girls' hostel near you love your chocolate cake. But it's ₹700, and most students have only ₹100 or ₹200.

screens.prompt: Hostel students love your ₹700 chocolate cake, but most have only ₹100 or ₹200 to spend. What should you offer them?

options.label: The whole cake at ₹600, for students
One slice at ₹90, in its own box

screens.why: Yes. A student with ₹100 can buy one slice today, like a worker buying one wash. She doesn't need to find 7 friends first.

wrong.a: ₹600 is still far more than ₹100 or ₹200. A small discount doesn't help. A small pack does.
wrong.c: It sounds fair, but one student must find 7 friends and collect money from each. Most won't. A slice she can buy alone is easier.

screens.prompt: Quick sum. Your 1 kg ₹700 cake cuts into 10 slices. Each sells for ₹90, and each box costs ₹10. Money left after boxes?
screens.why: Right. 10 × ₹90 = ₹900, minus 10 boxes × ₹10 = ₹100. That's ₹800, ₹100 more than the whole cake, for extra cutting and packing. Students pay more per gram, and they're happy to.

wrong.a: 10 × ₹90 = ₹900 is right, but each slice needs its own ₹10 box. ₹900 − ₹100 = ₹800.
wrong.c: ₹700 is the whole cake's price. Slices bring 10 × ₹90 = ₹900, minus ₹100 for boxes: ₹800.

screens.setup: It's May. You now make a ₹300 mini cake for 3 people. It leaves you ₹170 after costs. Your ₹700 birthday cake leaves you ₹350. Hostel students and two offices want small cakes for tea breaks. Some birthday families ask about the mini too.
screens.question: Where do you sell slices and mini cakes?

options.label: On your menu, for everyone
options.outcome: About 10 new buyers come. But 12 birthday families switch from the ₹700 cake to a ₹300 mini. Each switch costs you ₹350 − ₹170 = ₹180, so you lose ₹2,160 a month and gain about ₹1,700.
options.why: Small packs are for people who can't buy the big one. When your big-cake buyers choose the smaller one, you earn less from the same people.
options.better: Sell slices and minis only at the hostel and offices, not on your menu.

options.label: Only at the hostel and offices, not on your menu
options.outcome: Slices and minis sell at the hostel gate and to the two offices for tea breaks. Your menu for families shows only the ₹700 cake, and almost no birthday family switches. About 30 new buyers a month.
options.why: You used small packs to reach people who couldn't buy the big cake, and kept the big cake for people who could.

options.label: Nobody. Small orders are too much work
options.outcome: Your weeks stay simple, and your birthday cakes sell as before. The hostel students buy pastries from a shop near their gate.
options.why: Keeping things simple is fair, but many buyers who loved your cake still couldn't buy it.
options.better: Sell slices and minis only at the hostel and offices, not on your menu.

screens.text: People look at the price of one ___. A small pack lets people buy who can't pay for a ___ one.
screens.why: Exactly. A worker could buy one wash of Chik for 50 paise. A student can buy one slice of your cake for ₹90.

summary: The sachet idea: many buyers look at the price of one use, not the price per kilo.
A small pack lets people buy who can't pay for a big one, even if each gram costs a bit more.
Keep small packs for new buyers, so your big-pack buyers don't choose the smaller ones.

cards.front: A family has only ₹20 to spend. A jar of pickle is ₹120. What might let them buy?
cards.back: They look at the price of one use. A small pack lets them buy today.

cards.front: A 1 kg cake makes 10 slices. Each slice sells for ₹90 and its box costs ₹10. What do 10 slices bring after boxes?
Your ₹700 cake buyers start buying your ₹300 mini cake instead. Is that good?
options: No. You earn less from the same people
